Field surveys on Chaetodon citrinellus across the northern Great Barrier Reef during the austral summer recorded a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 6% [GSI = 6%] in females at a mean water temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. This measurement was derived from gravid individuals collected between November and January, a period of peak spawning activity for the species. The index reflects the proportion of body mass allocated to ovarian tissue and suggests a strategy of iteroparous spawning with repeated, relatively low-volume gamete releases over the extended breeding season. The local thermal regime, recorded consistently at 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C] during the collection window, falls within the optimal thermal range for gametogenesis in this species, supporting sustained vitellogenic activity during the summer months.

The maximum body size attained by Chaetodon citrinellus in the wild reaches an ultimate total length of 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters], a dimension consistent with the mid-range of sizes observed among the small-bodied butterflyfishes inhabiting Indo-Pacific coral reefs. This length was determined from a compilation of over three hundred individual length records taken during standardized underwater visual censuses conducted at Lizard Island and surrounding reef habitats. Individuals approaching this asymptotic size are typically those exceeding five years of age, displaying the characteristic deep-bodied, laterally compressed morphology that facilitates maneuverability within complex coral substrates. In comparison to sympatric species such as Chaetodon plebeius, which achieves a slightly smaller Li of roughly 11 centimeters, the speckled butterflyfish maintains a modest size advantage that may reflect differences in foraging niche, with C. citrinellus exhibiting a more generalized diet that includes both coral polyps and benthic invertebrates. The ultimate length of 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters] serves as a useful benchmark for estimating other life-history parameters, including the length-based approximations of body mass at various developmental stages.

Sexual maturation in this species is initiated once individuals attain a total length at puberty of 6.7 centimeters [Lp = 6.7 centimeters], a size threshold that typically corresponds to an age of roughly one to two years post-settlement based on otolith increment analyses. This length benchmark was established from histological examination of gonadal tissue in a size-stratified sample of fish collected from the lagoon systems of Moorea, French Polynesia. At 6.7 centimeters [Lp = 6.7 centimeters], individuals display the first unambiguous signs of gametogenic activity, including the onset of spermatogenesis in males and the appearance of cortical alveoli-stage oocytes in females. The attainment of this size represents a critical life-history transition, marking the shift from purely somatic growth to a phase where energy is partitioned toward both continued body expansion and the initial stages of reproductive allocation. Notably, the Lp value for Chaetodon citrinellus is relatively low compared to that of the larger-bodied obligate corallivore Chaetodon trifascialis, which does not mature until approximately 9.0 centimeters, suggesting that a more generalized diet may allow for an earlier onset of reproductive capability through more consistent nutrient intake during the juvenile phase. The length at first maturity appears to vary minimally across the species geographic range.

The wet weight at birth, derived from an average pelagic egg diameter of 0.75 millimeters, is calculated to be 0.00022 grams [Wwb = 0.00022 grams], a mass that reflects the lecithotrophic strategy typical of chaetodontid early life stages. Given the spherical geometry of the transparent, yolk-laden egg, each freshly spawned ovum contains just enough endogenous yolk reserves to sustain the embryo through the roughly 30-hour incubation period (approximately 30 hours) [ab = approximately 30 hours] required before eclosion occurs at 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C]. This brief but critical phase of endotrophic development sees the embryo reliant entirely on its maternally provisioned yolk sac, with the onset of first exogenous feeding occurring shortly after the mouth opens and the yolk reserves become exhausted. The tiny mass of the newly emerged yolk-sac larva, at just 0.00022 grams [Wwb = 0.00022 grams], places Chaetodon citrinellus among the many coral-reef teleosts that produce large numbers of small, pelagic offspring as part of a classic r-selected early life-history strategy. The age at birth (approximately 30 hours) [ab = approximately 30 hours] under these thermal conditions is consistent with the rapid developmental rates observed in tropical marine fishes, where elevated water temperatures accelerate embryogenesis considerably in comparison to temperate congeners at a temperature of 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C].

The asymptotic wet weight attained by adult Chaetodon citrinellus reaches 45.3 grams [Wwi = 45.3 grams], a mass derived from length-weight regressions applied to the maximum recorded total length of 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters]. In contrast, individuals at the onset of reproductive maturity, corresponding to a total length at puberty of 6.7 centimeters [Lp = 6.7 centimeters], achieve a wet weight at puberty of approximately 6.4 grams [Wwp = approximately 6.4 grams], reflecting the substantial allocation of resources toward gonadal development that occurs between these two size benchmarks. This nearly sevenfold increase in body mass from puberty to the asymptotic adult size underscores the extended period of somatic growth that characterizes this slow-growing, relatively long-lived species. Indeed, the maximum documented lifespan for Chaetodon citrinellus under natural conditions is 9,125 days [am = 9,125 days] at 28.3 °C [T = 28.3 °C], or roughly 25 years, a longevity that ranks among the highest recorded for butterflyfishes and that likely contributes to the species stable population structure observed in long-term monitoring studies on the Great Barrier Reef. The wet weight at puberty of 6.4 grams [Wwp = 6.4 grams] also provides a critical baseline for understanding the metabolic demands and foraging requirements necessary to sustain the species characteristic pair-bonding and territorial behaviors during the breeding season.
